description: Hi, I’m Maimuna, a CSE student interested in Computer Vision, AI, and Machine Learning. For NASA Space Apps, I want to tackle realistic problems through Earth and solar observation and build solutions that reach and benefit people. I’m looking for teammates skilled in ML/data science, frontend/backend development, Earth observation/GIS, and science communication.
summary: TERRALENS is a game that teaches people how satellite radar sees floods. Players pick a real flood (the Jamuna River in Bangladesh, the Brahmaputra in India, or the Solimões in Brazil). They compare radar images from before and after the flood on a swipe map, and mark the places where water has spread. The app checks their answers, gives them points and ranks, and explains why radar works through clouds. The goal is to make Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) easy to understand for students and the public.
details:
TERRALENS – Project Description

TERRALENS is a browser-based educational game that teaches people how to identify and map floodwater using real Sentinel-1 satellite radar data.
What it does: Radar sees through clouds and darkness, so it can map floods when ordinary cameras can’t. TERRALENS turns this into a mission-based game.

Core gameplay

  • Three missions, unlocked by XP:
    1. The Changing Jamuna River (Bangladesh), unlocked from the start.
    2. Brahmaputra Flood Surge (Assam, India), unlocked at 100 XP.
    3. Amazon Wetland Dynamics (Manaus, Brazil), unlocked at 250 XP.
  • Each mission has a story, a pre-flood and post-flood date, and an estimated area.
  • Radar Lab:

    This is the main screen. You step through a timeline of real radar scenes, compare before and after, and mark where you think new floodwater is. Your marks are scored against an in-browser change-detection result.
  • Briefing and conclusion: Each mission opens with a briefing. You then write your own conclusion and answer impact questions, and these earn bonus XP.

Benefits and intended impact:

  • Anyone with a browser can learn how SAR works with real data, with no GIS software or remote-sensing background.
  • It builds the skills behind flood mapping, which humanitarian and disaster-response teams use in practice.
  • It is honest about uncertainty. The code and interface state that results are threshold-based observations of new water, not confirmed flooding. Smooth dry sand can look like water, and flooded vegetation can look like land. The fixed threshold is a starting point, not a calibration. We think teaching these limits matters as much as teaching the method.

Tools and technologies:

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, React Router, MapLibre GL JS, maplibre-gl-compare, Terra Draw, Lucide icons.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, SQLite, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, HTTPX, and the ASF hyp3_sdk.
  • Data processing: Sentinel-1 radiometric terrain correction (RTC) at 10 m resolution, change detection by thresholding and connected-component filtering, and unit tests with Python unittest.

Creativity:

  • It frames real Earth observation analysis as a mission-based investigation game instead of a static dashboard.
  • It combines in-browser analysis on real satellite tiles with a server-side game layer.
  • It uses an offline-capable design and includes the method’s known limits in the interface.

Factors we considered:

  • Accuracy and honesty about what SAR water detection can and cannot show.
  • Accessibility and low barriers: it runs in a browser and works without the backend.
  • Using VH instead of VV for the in-browser analysis, because wind-roughened water can rise above a VV threshold and make the river disappear on windy dates.
  • Terrain and latitude effects on pixel area, so area estimates use true ground area.
  • Cheating prevention: answers are checked and XP is capped on the server.
  • Public, freely available data so anyone can reproduce the results.
